newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU faces barley rebate pressure after Saudi deal.
newsitem.headline: EU faces barley rebate pressure after Saudi deal.

text.p: Canada and Australia are likely to win the lion's share of a large sale of feed barley to Saudi Arabia, unless the European Union sharply steps up its barley export rebate, EU grain exporters said on Thursday.

Saudi Arabia has bought 500,000 tonnes of optional-origin feed barley at prices ranging from $154-$156 per tonne, cost and freight, exporters said on Wednesday. The barley is for delivery until January 31 to the Gulf port of Dammam.

Most of the business is expected to go to Canada and Australia, countries which enjoy a freight advantage over EU barley to that destination, they said. "The EU may not do one single tonne of barley," one trader said.
"I expect most of the business to go to Canada and Australia, with possibly 50,000 tonnes going to the EU," another trader said.
Traders put freight costs for EU barley to Dammam at $25 per tonne against $21 for Australian and Canadian barley.
One exporter estimated that EU barley was worth around $133 per tonne, fob. Including freight and other costs, this put EU barley at a little over $160 per tonne against $154 for Australian barley.
One trader estimated that the EU would need to raise its refund on barley exports to 35-36 Ecus per tonne from a current level of 31.49 Ecus in order to participate in the deal.
But the EU may be reluctant to comply as it has already taken part in two large sales of feed barley to the Saudis and is under less pressure to export its bumper barley crop.
Traders estimated that the EU had already sold close to 50 percent of potential barley exports of 6.5 million tonnes for the 1996/97 season.
Exporters also expect the Saudis, who have covered their import requirements until end January, to shop again for barley next year.
They put Saudi Arabia's import needs at around 400,000-500,000 tonnes per month.
